newsitem.title: UK: Italy's EMU fate poses problem for rest of union.
newsitem.headline: Italy's EMU fate poses problem for rest of union.

text.p: Italy is on course to fulfil as many of the rules for entry into Europe's single currency club as Germany, according to a Reuters survey.
But analysts said Rome's entry would probably have to be delayed because of the weight of German public opinion against a euro which includes the lira from the start.
But they said Italian exclusion could raise as many problems as it solves, with the possibility of a revolt from Rome and other near-miss countries jeopardising the launch of EMU.

According to the survey of 32 economists across Europe, both Italy and Germany are expected to meet the inflation, interest rate and exchange rate criteria in 1997 as laid down in the Maastricht Treaty for entry to EMU.

But both look like failing on the size of their budget deficit and debt ratios. According to Maastricht, a country's budget deficit must be no greater than three percent of its GDP in 1997, and the debt-to-GDP ratio must be 60 percent or less.

With no country able to meet all of the entry criteria, it is almost certain that the rules will be relaxed. This paves the way for countries such as Italy to join, although it is feared their presence will undermine the euro's strength at its birth.

"Chancellor (Helmut) Kohl has to sell the single currency to the German people. To do that Italy would have to be excluded for a couple of years," said one contributor to the poll, which was conducted between February 5 and 10.
Portugal and Spain are also expected to meet and fail the same criteria as Italy, but analysts believe it will be more difficult to exclude them from EMU in 1999.

A Reuters survey published on Friday showed that only seven percent of the experts taking part thought Italy would be in from the start, while 31 percent forecast Spain as a founder member and 29 percent predicted Portugal would be included.

"Policy in Spain and Portugal in the last few years has been completely geared towards meeting EMU criteria, they will not accept no for an answer," said Felix Gonzalez, chief economist at Beta Capital in Spain.
"If a decision is made to exclude Italy, Spain and Portugal, then the majority voting rules could be used with the help of one other country to derail the EMU project," said Gonzalez.
Each country has a weighted vote, based loosely on the size of it's economy. Italy has 10, Spain eight and Portugal five.
There are 87 votes in total, with 62 needed for a qualified majority. If a group of countries can come up 26 votes, they could theoretically stop EMU from going ahead in 1999.

A solution along the lines of Italy waiting for a couple of years, but setting the lira at a fixed rate against the euro until becoming a full member, would go some way to overcoming German reservations, some analysts said.
"The market would see this as a viable solution and it would allow Kohl to present the euro as a solid currency to the German public," said Rob Hayward, economist at Bank of America.
Last week Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, meeting Kohl to push for Italy's founder membership of EMU, said the lira would have to be devalued if Italy did not join from the start.
Such a move would put French and German exporters at a competitive disadvantage, which some analysts said would bring France into Italy's pro-membership lobby.

France may also support Italy to act as a counterweight against Germany, whose monetary policy currently sends strong ripples through Europe -- Bundesbank interest rate changes tend to be followed by other European countries to avoid disruption in their own economies and maintain currency levels.
"Italy would provide an ally against Germany in making sure that the European central bank (ECB) sets monetary policy along the lines the French want," said Hayward.
"France would like to see a more expansionist and interventionist policy. If the ECB is going to be a clone of the Bundesbank then it's all been for nothing."
